profile.summary: Joshua narrates the transition from Israel's leadership after Moses to Joshua, his former auxiliary, and the entry of the people into the promised land. The book describes the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the advance through the central and northern regions of Canaan, and the distribution of the land among the tribes. His central message is that God fulfills his promises faithfully, while judging sin with seriousness. The work was most likely composed after Joshua's death, although it can preserve personal memories and accounts of witnesses, and its final form is generally situated at least in Israel's initial monarchy.
profile.setting: The narrative takes place after the forty years of pilgrimage in the desert, when a new generation of Israelites, now willing to trust in God's promises, is ready to enter Canaan. The geographical setting includes the region east of the Jordan, the Jordan Valley, the central plateau, the Galilee hills, the Neguebe and the coastal plain. Canaan was made up of small city-states often linked in unstable coalitions, first to the south and then to the north, without preventing Israel's advance. The book shows Israel coming out of Acacia, crossing the Jordan, conquering Jericho and the center of the land, and then occupying the territories already open for settlement.

structure.label: Preparation for entry to the ground
structure.description: Joshua is confirmed as leader and Israel is preparing to cross the Jordan and take possession of the promised land.

structure.label: Conquest of the earth
structure.description: It includes the fall of Jericho, the episode of Achan, the victory over cananeian coalitions of the south and north, and the advance that paves the way for the settlement in the mountainous country.

structure.label: Start of territorial distribution
structure.description: The introductory section of inheritances and the initial highlight for Caleb mark the beginning of the land distribution.

structure.label: Distribution of the tribes
structure.description: The portions attributed, with special attention to Judah, Benjamin and Joseph, are described, in addition to the closure of this section with Joshua's inheritance.

structure.label: Community provisions on land
structure.description: The cities of refugee are separated and cities attributed to the Levites within the tribal territories.

structure.label: Return of the eastern tribes and resolution of a misunderstanding
structure.description: The two and a half tribes who received land east of the Jordan return, after a tension solved with the western tribes.

structure.label: Final speeches and closure
structure.description: Joshua bids farewell to the people, summons the renewal of the covenant and the book concludes with striking funerals.

themes: Fidelity of God to the promises of the covenant
Holiness of God and the seriousness of sin
Memory and teaching for future generations
Possession of the earth as a gift of God, not human merit
Inclusion and recognition of faithful people such as Raab, Caleb and the daughters of Zelophehad
readingKeys: Notice how the text alternates conquest, obedience, and judgment, showing that military victory and spiritual fidelity walk together.
Notice the stone memorials and the final farewells as signs of historical and theological teaching for the following generations.
Read the division of the earth not only as a geographical list, but as a concrete testimony of the fulfillment of the promises made to the patriarchs.
profile.cautions: The human authorship of the book is not explicitly claimed in the text itself and is traditionally considered anonymous; the final form is after Joshua's death, although it may preserve ancient materials and memories of witnesses. The book presents only the great contours of the entrance and conquest, not saying that all the Canaanites were eliminated. Reading should take to serious both the narrated judgments and the prophetic perspective of the work, without forcing the text beyond what the introduction provides.

dossier.narratedEra: Joshua's narrative lies in the transition between the end of Moses' leadership and Israel's entry into Canaan, with the crossing of the Jordan, the campaigns against Canaanite coalitions, the conquest of Jericho, and the distribution of the land among the tribes. The notes place this world in a scene of Canadian state-city, variable military alliances and a newly outgoing Israeli population of forty years in the desert.
dossier.compositionEra: The secondary introductions used here distinguish the narrated time from the composition. They claim that the book was written after Joshua's death, with allusions such as "today" and the Book of Jasir indicating a later essay; at the same time, they suggest that part of the material may derive from personal memories or records of Joshua and his subordinates. Matthew Henry speculates on a later prophetic collection, possibly in final form prior to the initial or reunited monarchy later, but this appears as a conjecture, not as sure.

politics.title: Cities-state Canaanite and military coalitions
politics.detail: Canaan is described as organized into small city-states, each with its king, gathered in mutable coalitions. The notes highlight that the southern coalition and then the northern coalition were the closest to a total unit among the Canaanites.
politics.readingImpact: This makes reading Joshua's campaigns less as a war against a unified empire and more as successive clashes against regional power networks; it also helps to understand why the Israeli victory appears as decisive even though Israel is numerically smaller.

politics.title: Deans defeated as political expression of divine judgment
politics.detail: The list of overdue kings in Joshua 12 is presented as a record of the defeated "reinos" or city-states, linking their collapse to God's purpose and prolonged judgment on the Canaanites.
politics.readingImpact: Attention to the catalogue of kings shows that conquest is narrated as a political reordering of the territory under divine initiative, not only as episodic military victories.

politics.title: Eastern Tribe and Trans-Drocratic Military Obligations
politics.detail: Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh received land east of the Jordan and their warriors were to cross the river to fight with the rest of Israel before returning to their possessions.
politics.readingImpact: The context clarifies that Israel's political unity was still being negotiated: there would be different lands, but a common obligation of war and loyalty to the whole people.

politics.title: Joshua Authority and Leadership Transition
politics.detail: The notes show Joshua as the successor of Moses and chief delegate to fulfill the promise of the earth; disobeying the chosen leader by God is treated as treason against God Himself.
politics.readingImpact: The narrative must be read with a strong burden of political-sacral legitimacy: leadership is not only administrative, but representative of divine authority.

politics.title: Meeting in Shechem as a peaceful renewal of the community
politics.detail: In Joshua 24, the assembly in Shechem takes the form of a treaty of suzerainty-vasage: preamble, historical delivery, stipulations, blessings/curses, witnesses and deposit of the text.
politics.readingImpact: This guides the reading of the final chapter as a public political-covenantal act, in which the national life of Israel is reaffirmed under the exclusive lordship of the Lord.

customs.title: Camp, crossing and entry by stages on earth
customs.detail: The narrative mentions the beginning in Acacia Grove/Acazias in the Transjordão, the crossing of the Jordan and the entry into Canaan by the eastern route, after the unbelieving generation died in the desert.
customs.readingImpact: The background highlights a generational and logistical transition: the people do not "surge" on earth, but arrive after a long wait and community reorganization.

customs.title: Agrarian life and settlement in conquered regions
customs.detail: The notes say that obedience to the law would allow the people to establish productive farms, houses, towns and cities in the occupied territory.
customs.readingImpact: The conquest does not end in military victory; it paves the way for an agricultural and sedentary everyday life, which gives practical weight to fidelity to God's instruction.

customs.title: Spying, Hospitality and Family Protection in Jericho
customs.detail: Two young spies enter Jericho and are helped by Rahab, who obtains promise of preservation for themselves and his family in exchange for their cooperation.
customs.readingImpact: The episode shows how family alliances and domestic shelter can become means of survival and grace, reversing cultural expectations about who deserves protection.

customs.title: Memorials of stone as public catechesis
customs.detail: Joshua erected and/or had memorial stones raised at various times; they served as visual signs to teach future generations about God's faithfulness.
customs.readingImpact: The text should be read with attention to the culture of material memory: worship and instruction depend not only on words, but on visible milestones in the common space.

customs.title: Destination of inheritances, cities of refuge and Levites
customs.detail: The second half of the book deals with the territorial distribution between tribes, with cities of refuge and Levitical cities inserted within the tribal territories.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the land was organized not only by borders, but by social and religious functions; the possession of the land was accompanied by community responsibilities.

customs.title: Honorific sections as a mark of belonging to the land
customs.detail: The closure highlights the burials of Joshua, Eleazar, and the translation of Joseph's bones to Canaan; the notes compare this to the contrast with Abraham, who had to buy a piece of land to bury Sarah.
customs.readingImpact: The funerary culture becomes theological argument: burials in Canaan function as a concrete proof that the promise has been fulfilled and that the land now belongs to the descendants of the promise.

language.title: Repetition of strong and courageous care as a rhetorical emphasis
language.detail: God repeats to Joshua the need to be strong and courageous three times in Joshua 1, in a chain of encouragement and demand.
language.readingImpact: The repetition signals that Joshua's leadership requires moral and spiritual constancy, not mere military skill.

language.title: Book of Instruction and centrality of the torah
language.detail: The note identifies the "Book of Instruction" probably with Deuteronomy, covering legal codes and moral and spiritual instructions.
language.readingImpact: This guides the reading of Joshua 1:8 as a call to continuous meditation in divine instruction, not as simple formal observance of rules.

language.title: Alliance formulations in old legal language
language.detail: Joshua 24 is described as similar to an ancient treaty of suzerainty-vassala, with preamble, historical prologue, clauses, witnesses, and deposit of the document.
language.readingImpact: Language shows that the final chapter is not only devotional; it formalizes community obligations in a legal and public record.

language.title: I'd... I... dei... send... brought..." as the theological cadence
language.detail: In Joshua 24, the repetition of the divine verbs emphasizes that Israel's faith is a response to God's initiative.
language.readingImpact: The verbal form shapes the message: the history of Israel is read as a sequence of divine acts before it is a human achievement.

language.title: "Today" as a later writing mark
language.detail: Matthew Henry notes that expressions such as "today," in addition to references to sources such as the Book of Jasar, suggest additions or editorial update after the narrated events.
language.readingImpact: The reader must distinguish between the event itself and the final literary form of the text, which preserves historical memory with later editing marks.

language.title: "Cut covenant" and the materiality of the covenant
language.detail: The literal expression "cutting an alliance" is mentioned for Joshua 24:25, and the witness stone is treated as possibly inscribed monument.
language.readingImpact: The language reinforces that the alliance is something solemnly ratified, with legal weight and physical memorial, not just an inner commitment.

timeline.title: Forty years in the desert before entry
timeline.detail: The previous generation refused to enter the land; as a consequence, Israel remained forty years in the desert until a new generation came ready to trust in the divine promises.
timeline.readingImpact: The narrated time is interpreted as a formative discipline: the entry into Canaan succeeds a period of unbelief and generational substitution.

timeline.title: Death of Moses and commissioning of Joshua
timeline.detail: The notes place the death of Moses on Mount Nebo, east of the Jordan, and place the commissioning of Joshua immediately afterwards.
timeline.readingImpact: This marks the beginning of the narrative as a succession of leadership, not as a new independent project; Joshua continues the promise given to Moses.

timeline.title: Crossing Jordan and Campaigns of Conquest
timeline.detail: The first half of the book describes the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the setback caused by Achan, the defeat of the southern coalition and after the north.
timeline.readingImpact: The internal chronology shows a step forward: entry, moral crisis, victory in the south and consolidation in the north.

timeline.title: Approximate borders of Joshua's conquests
timeline.detail: Joshua 12 summarizes the conquests from the Arnon to the south/east, to Baal-Gad and Mount Hermon to the north, with Mount Halak marking the southern boundary in Western Canaan.
timeline.readingImpact: Borders help to read the book as a selective account of broad territorial domain, but not necessarily of total occupation.

timeline.title: Distribution of land and central inheritances
timeline.detail: The second half concentrates on the territorial distribution between the tribes, with emphasis on Judah, Benjamin and Joseph, as well as the inheritances of Caleb and Joshua and the cities of refuge.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology of the book changes from war to settlement, showing that the conquest culminates in social and cultual organization of the land.

timeline.title: Final writing before or near the initial monarchy, according to the notes
timeline.detail: Tyndale claims it is likely that Joshua existed in more or less current form at most until the initial monarchy; Matthew Henry conjecturally speaks of later compilation by prophets, and possibly editorial closure in the pre-exile or post-exlicic period.
timeline.readingImpact: This prevents confusing the time of events with the time of the final form of the book: the text preserves ancient traditions, but was organized editorially afterwards.

investigation: The notes do not definitively resolve the human authorship of the book; Tyndale claims anonymity and Matthew Henry presents traditional and conjectural hypotheses.

The historical discussion is selective: Tyndale defends general reliability and responds to archaeological objections about Transjordan, Jericho and Ai, but also admits that the book offers only the general lines of the entrance to Canaan.
There is a tension between confessional reading and academic debate: the book is treated as a selective history, in a prophetic perspective, without claiming exhaustiveness.
The sources mention canane coalitions, state-city and continuation of Canaanites on earth, but do not describe in detail the entire chronology of the subsequent occupation.
The reference to the Book of Jasar, the expressions "today" and possible editorial additions support later composition, but does not allow to fix exact date.
The final section uses an old treatise mold; this is an explicit literary comparison of the notes, not proof independent of a specific diplomatic event.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the provided notes and therefore depends on the selective coverage of them. Some important areas for Joshua's study appear only indirectly: economics, social classes, meals, everyday work and cult details are mentioned only when notes touch on land, cities, memorials or alliances. It was not possible to develop an exact chronology of writing, because the sources offer only probable intervals, conjectures and debates on later editing. Nor should this summary be read as an independent historical proof: when the notes say that something is "probable," "possible," or "debated," the dossier preserves this caution. Finally, confessional readings of the sources are kept in a contextual perspective, without trying to harmonize all critical or archaeological issues outside of what was explicitly stated.
